text.L1: Fractions are numbers, so they have places on a number line.
text.L2: The bottom number tells how many equal gaps to make from 0 to 1.
text.L3: Count gaps, not marks. Four marks between 0 and 1 make five equal gaps.
text.L4: So each gap is one fifth. The top number tells how many gaps to count from 0.
text.L5: To mark two fifths, count two gaps from 0. That mark is 2/5.
text.L6: A fraction can also go beyond 1. If the top number is bigger than the bottom number, it lies past 1.
text.L7: For example, 5/4 is one quarter past 1, so it is after 1.
text.L8: Now use these ideas to choose where 5/4 belongs.

els.text: A wrong prediction wastes the test

text.L1: Science is not just a list of facts to memorise. It is a way of finding out by observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
text.L2: Start by noticing something. Ask a question that you can answer by doing something and observing or measuring what happens.
text.L3: Before the test, make a prediction. It is a guess with a reason, based on what you already know.
text.L4: For example, ask whether curd sets faster in a warm place or a cool place. Predict that the warm bowl will set first because the starter bacteria work faster in warmth.
text.L5: Test fairly with the same milk, the same amount and the same starter. Keep one bowl warm and one bowl cool, then observe and record them after the same time.
text.L6: The result may support the prediction or may not. A wrong prediction is still useful because it teaches us something new and leads to another question.
text.L7: Remember the circle: observe, ask, predict, test and conclude. Then use what you learned to ask a new question.

L4.text: For example, ask whether curd sets faster in a warm place or a cool place. Predict that the warm bowl will set first because the starter bacteria work faster in warmth.

L5.text: Test fairly with the same milk, the same amount and the same starter. Keep one bowl warm and one bowl cool, then observe and record them after the same time.

L6.text: The result may support the prediction or may not. A wrong prediction is still useful because it teaches us something new and leads to another question.

L7.text: Remember the circle: observe, ask, predict, test and conclude. Then use what you learned to ask a new question.

task.prompt: Put the steps of finding out in order, starting with noticing something.
